blocking_rules.description: Same surname and same first initial. This is the rule that finds most pairs.
blocking_rules._measured: 26,958 pairs over 9,678 blocks on the September 2026 sheet. The biggest block held 141 units.

blocking_rules.description: The surname sounds the same and the forename maps to the same canonical form. This rescues SMITH against SMYTH, and BILL against WILLIAM.
Same forename, and the surname starts with the same letter. This catches a surname that changed or was mistyped.
blocking_rules._measured: 76,738 pairs on the September 2026 sheet: the most expensive of the three rules, and still far inside the budget.

comparisons.description: Forename after the nickname lookup, so ROBERT and BOB have already met. Two Jaro-Winkler levels below exact.
Surname. A rare surname counts for more than a common one, so agreeing on FOTHERGILL is stronger evidence than agreeing on SMITH.
Middle names. Most records carry none, so most pairs land on the missing-value level and are neither helped nor punished.
comparisons._measured: 4,788 of 13,310 person units carry a middle name.

comparisons.description: The title the cleaning stripped off the name. Weak on its own; it mainly separates a MR from a MRS of the same name.

em_blocking_rules: l.forename_canon = r.forename_canon AND l.parties = r.parties AND l.units = r.units AND l.title = r.title
person._em_note: The second rule is the one that trains the surname comparison, so it must not name the surname. It also has to be tight enough for EM to tell matches from non-matches inside the block. Blocking on the forename alone made 820,068 training pairs, 97% with different surnames and only 6.5% true matches, and EM concluded that half of all true matches have a different surname (m 0.479 for 'not the same'; the sheet's own labels say 0.000). Adding the recipient party, the accounting unit and the title narrows the block to 14,583 pairs at a 45% match rate. Those three columns are not compared, so blocking on them switches nothing off. Measured on the September 2026 sheet: m 0.0015, surname mismatch now costs 9.4 bits instead of 1.1, review queue 1,235 to 713, pair recall 62.4% to 64.2%, pair precision 98.7% to 98.3%. If this block ever gets thin on a future sheet, drop the parties clause: it blocks 31,592 pairs for the same result.
person._name_clean_note: A cl.JaroWinklerAtThresholds comparison on name_clean was tried here and taken out again. It did break up the 0.70-0.80 spike, but by inflating every score: name_clean contains the forename and the surname, which are already comparisons of their own, and Splink assumes its comparisons are independent, so the same evidence was counted twice. Person pair precision fell 0.9872 -> 0.9008 (score_only), the review queue went from 1,059 pairs to 29,121, and no pair scored below 0.5 at all. Recall did rise 0.6236 -> 0.8899. The honest fix for the spike is evidence the name does not already carry - the donation amount profile and the recipients - which is what the GBT in slice 5 is for.

blocking_rules._measured: 6,033 pairs. It was 90,730 until the placeholder postcodes were made missing: 412 units all carried ZZ0 0ZZ, which alone made 84,666 of them.

blocking_rules.description: Same padded company number. Nearly everything this rule finds, the match keys have already put together.
Same first word of the core name and same postcode district. This rescues an organisation that was renamed or re-suffixed at one address.

comparisons.description: The name with the legal form taken off. The main signal on this track.
Sorted distinct words of the core name, compared on overlap. Catches a different word order and a dropped word.
Postcode at full, sector, district and area level, so a nearby address still counts for something.
Padded company number. Strong when present; absent on most donations rows.
The suffix the cleaning split off — LTD, LLP, PLC. Weak, and mainly separates a company from a union of the same name.

_accept_line_measured: The two tracks want different accept lines, so the person track sets its own and the organisation track reads the shared 0.92. Measured on the September 2026 sheet after the second EM training rule was tightened (donations_surname_em_2026-09-22.md, 'Accept line sweep'). Person: 0.96 is the lowest line that clears the precision the shipped configuration had. It reaches 0.98770 against 0.98720, and the recall it costs is 0.0009 — about a tenth of the 0.0184 the training fix gained. 0.95 reaches only 0.98619 and falls short. Organisation: the same move would cost 0.0054 of recall for a precision gain of 0.0047, roughly two correct merges lost for each wrong one prevented, and it would take organisation pairs in the review band from 176 to 362. So the organisation line stays at 0.92.
_notes: Pair counts are from the units of the September 2026 donations sheet (13,310 person units, 9,125 organisation). Each track's rules cost about 128,000 pairs (person) and 11,000 (organisation), so max_pairs of 5,000,000 leaves plenty of headroom while still stopping a rule that blocks on a near-constant column. probability_two_random_records_match is null, so Splink estimates it from that track's match keys at the recall in deterministic_recall.
